title: The Threefold World and the Vanity of All Sciences: Agrippa from Cologne to Grenoble
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cologne, birth in the colony of Agrippina
stops.date_confidence: attested: 14 September 1486 is given by the Stanford Encyclopedia entry and by the German and French Wikipedia articles alike. Birthplace contested. Three of the four sources say Cologne outright and the French article derives the surname from Colonia Agrippina; only the English article's infobox says Nettersheim, which is a different Eifel village from the Nettesheim of the family name. Cologne is followed here and the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of September a son is born to a family of Cologne burghers, in the city the Romans founded as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium. The name he will print on the front of every book is taken from the city itself: Agrippa, of Cologne. The 'von Nettesheim' he adds later is a family toponym, a village name inherited rather than a place he came out of. The household is comfortable enough to send him to the university at thirteen, and settled enough that the boy is entered on the rolls as a citizen of Cologne, not as a countryman come in from the Rhineland.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim' (Vittoria Perrone Compagni)
suggested_refs: The University of Cologne matriculation register, which calls him a citizen of Cologne

stops.name: Nettesheim, the village behind the name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the village is the source of the surname, not an attested birthplace, and no source consulted places his birth here. Coordinates are Nettesheim in the municipality of Rommerskirchen, Rhein-Kreis Neuss (51.035, 6.691), and deliberately not the Eifel village of Nettersheim, roughly 40 km south, with which the two names are regularly confused. The date repeats the birth date only to hold the stop in place.
stops.campa: North-west of Cologne, in the flat beet country of what is now Rommerskirchen, sits the village of Nettesheim. It gives him the second half of the name under which every printed edition of his work will appear: Henricus Cornelius Agrippa ab Nettesheym. Whether he was ever carried there as an infant, no record says. Later editors went looking for a birthplace to match the name and found Nettersheim instead, a different village forty kilometres to the south, in the Eifel. That is the one the English infobox prints.
sources: Wikipedia (en), 'Rommerskirchen' (Nettesheim redirect, 51 degrees 2 minutes 5 seconds N, 6 degrees 41 minutes 29 seconds E)
suggested_refs: The two villages, Nettesheim in Rommerskirchen and Nettersheim in the Eifel, and four centuries of editors conflating them

stops.name: Cologne, matriculation at thirteen
stops.date_confidence: attested: the matriculation record is cited by the English Wikipedia article and by the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology; the German article gives the baccalaureate in 1500 and the master of arts in 1502. His age at matriculation is inferred from the 1486 birth year. No month or day is recorded, so January is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: At about thirteen he matriculates in the arts faculty at Cologne, the great Thomist university of the Rhineland, and works the trivium under masters for whom Albertus Magnus is the house authority. What the faculty hands him is the scholastic method, which he will spend the rest of his life using against scholastics, and a Latin good enough to lecture in anywhere from Franche-Comte to Piedmont. The baccalaureate comes in 1500 and the master of arts in 1502. He is sixteen years old when he takes it, and there is no post waiting.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The arts faculty of the University of Cologne c.1500 and its Albertist curriculum

stops.name: Paris, the sodalitium of the Latin Quarter
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was in Paris in these years (Stanford Encyclopedia); the bracket c.1502-1507 is that chronology's. The character of the circle is disputed between sources, and the named membership given in specialist literature is not confirmed by any page consulted and is therefore not asserted here. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: After the master's degree he is in Paris, among young men who read Hebrew, alchemy, and the newly printed Hermetic books together. From this circle he will be sent to Spain, to Dole, to London, always on somebody else's business and usually with two or three of the same friends attached. The letters show the network and say nothing about its purpose. The Stanford chronology calls the group a sodalitium, a fellowship of humanist friends. The English article calls it a secret society.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Agrippa's printed Epistolae, the only surviving trace of the Paris circle

stops.name: Valencia, the Spanish business
stops.date_confidence: attested that the journey happened, and that it ran 1508-1509, per the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology; purpose and employer are unrecoverable from the surviving correspondence and no source consulted attempts a reconstruction. The Valencia-to-Lyon itinerary is given only by the English Wikipedia article, without sourcing, and is treated as reconstruction. Valencia is used as the pin because it is the only named starting point.
stops.campa: In 1508 and 1509 he crosses into Spain with two of the Paris associates, on business nobody has been able to reconstruct: military, political, or both, for an employer the letters never name. The English article strings out an itinerary of Valencia, the Balearics, Sardinia, Naples, Avignon, Lyon, without saying how it knows any of it. He comes back north with a reputation for being useful in matters that cannot be written down. The Stanford chronology gives the two years and nothing inside them.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The opacity of the 1508-1509 Spanish episode in every reconstruction of Agrippa's life

segments.name: Dole, Wurzburg, and the Book Written Young

stops.name: Dole, lecturing on De verbo mirifico
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology and the German Wikipedia article both give the 1509 Dole lectures on Reuchlin and the composition there of De nobilitate et praecellentia foeminei sexus under Margaret of Austria's nominal patronage. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: At Dole in Franche-Comte, on Habsburg ground, he lectures publicly on Johann Reuchlin's De verbo mirifico, the book that carried Christian Kabbalah into Latin Europe: the hidden power of the divine names, the Hebrew letters read as a Christology. It is his first public teaching and his first courtship of a patron. For Margaret of Austria, the regent, he composes a declamation on the nobility and pre-eminence of the female sex, arguing woman's superiority from Genesis and from Hebrew etymology. He is twenty-three years old and he is asking for a salary.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Johann Reuchlin, De verbo mirifico (1494)
Agrippa, De nobilitate et praecellentia foeminei sexus, composed at Dole 1509, printed 1529

stops.name: Wurzburg, the winter with the abbot
stops.date_confidence: attested: the visit in the winter of 1509-1510 is given by the English Wikipedia article and is already written and sourced on Trithemius's own file. Coordinates are the Schottenkloster St James's in the Mainviertel on the left bank (49.7957, 9.9205), inherited byte-identically from johannes_trithemius.journey.json, and not the right-bank point that circulates in synthesis. The Paracelsus tutelage at the same abbey c.1508 is tradition, not document, and the two men are nowhere recorded as having met.
stops.campa: He rides to Wurzburg in the winter and stays several days at the Schottenkloster, the abbey of the Irish monks, with Johannes Trithemius: cryptographer, chronicler, and compiler of catalogues listing books that never existed. They talk about chemistry, magic, and Kabbalah. Trithemius, who by one tradition has already taken in a young Swiss called Paracelsus, listens to a twenty-three-year-old propose that the whole of magic can be set out as one ordered science, and tells him to go and write it down. The draft is finished inside four months.
stops.quote: When I was of late (most reverend Father) for a while conversant with you in your Monastery of Herbipolis, we conferred together of divers things concerning Chymistry, Magick, and Cabalie, and of other things, which as yet lye hid in Secret Sciences, and Arts.
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, dedicatory letter to Johannes Trithemius, printed with De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: johannes_trithemius.journey.json, stop 'Wurzburg, the winter with Agrippa'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, prefatory correspondence, trans. John French (1651)
suggested_refs: The Schottenkloster St James's, Wurzburg, today the Don-Bosco-Kirche, Schottenanger

stops.name: Dole, the chair lost to a sermon preached at Ghent
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Franciscan provincial Jean Catilinet denounced him as a judaizing heretic and that the Dole position ended in consequence (Stanford Encyclopedia; German Wikipedia). The sermon was preached at the Habsburg court in GHENT, not at Dole as several syntheses have it, and the sources consulted contradict each other on exactly this point. Agrippa was absent, so the scene is narrated where he was. No source gives a year; March 1510 is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: While he is out of Franche-Comte the Franciscan provincial Jean Catilinet preaches the Lenten sermons at the Habsburg court in Ghent and denounces him from the pulpit as a judaizing heretic: the Reuchlin lectures, the Hebrew, the interest in names. Margaret of Austria hears it. The Dole position ends. Agrippa is not in the room and has no chance to answer. He answers years later anyway, in writing, in an Expostulatio addressed to Catilinet by name. No source consulted gives the year of the sermon.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Agrippa, Expostulatio super Expositione sua in librum De verbo mirifico cum Joanne Catilineti

stops.name: Wurzburg, the letter of the eighth of April
stops.date_confidence: attested: the dedicatory letter of 8 April 1510 is given by the English Wikipedia article and the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology, and both sides of the exchange are printed as prefatory matter in the 1651 English edition. The quote below is by Trithemius, about how to handle Agrippa's project, not by Agrippa. Pin inherited from johannes_trithemius.journey.json.
stops.campa: He sends Trithemius the finished draft, three books, with a dedicatory letter dated the eighth of April. Book one is the elemental world, book two the celestial, book three the intellectual, and every power in each is drawn down out of the one above it. Trithemius writes back praising the work and attaching a warning about who may be told what. Agrippa keeps that letter for twenty-three years and prints it at the front of the book when the book finally appears.
stops.quote: Give Hey to an Ox, Sugar to a Parret only; understand my meaning, least you be trod under the Oxens feet
stops.quote_source: Johannes Trithemius, reply to Agrippa (1510), printed as prefatory correspondence to De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, prefatory correspondence, trans. John French (1651)
johannes_trithemius.journey.json, stop 'Wurzburg, the letter of the eighth of April'
suggested_refs: The 1510 manuscript draft of De occulta philosophia, circulated in copies for twenty-three years before print

stops.name: London, the Pauline epistles with Colet
stops.date_confidence: attested that he travelled to England in 1510 on a political and secret assignment in imperial service, and that he met John Colet there (Stanford Encyclopedia; French Wikipedia). NOT attested: that he attended lectures, or in what building. The German article puts the lectures at Oxford, which is chronologically doubtful, since Colet's Oxford Pauline lectures fall c.1497-1504 and by 1510 he was Dean of St Paul's in London. No building is asserted; the pin is generic London. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He crosses to England on what the sources call a political and secret assignment in imperial service, and while he is there he studies the letters of Paul with John Colet, the Englishman who reads scripture as a document with a human author writing to particular people at a particular time. It is the exact opposite of the discipline he practises: no hidden name, no numerical value, only grammar and circumstance. He writes commentaries on the epistles in England. None of them survives.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: John Colet's Pauline exegesis and the English humanist reading of scripture c.1500

stops.name: Trieste, the emperor's war chest
stops.date_confidence: attested by the German Wikipedia article. The imperial service of these years is documented only in outline; specific duties, dates within the year, and payments are not recoverable. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He carries an imperial war chest to Trieste for Maximilian I, one more errand in a decade of errands whose paper trail is thin and whose payments seem never to have arrived in full. Northern Italy is at war with itself and with France, and a German with Latin, discretion, and no fixed loyalty can find work on any side of it. He will spend seven years in this country, lecturing when a university will have him and soldiering when none will. What the money was for, and whether he was ever paid his own share of it, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Maximilian I's Italian campaigns of the War of the League of Cambrai

stops.name: Pisa, the council against the pope
stops.date_confidence: attested that he attended the schismatic council at Pisa at the end of 1511 (German Wikipedia). The excommunication is reported there only on Agrippa's own testimony, 'nach eigenem Bekunden', and as a blanket measure taken against a great many theologians rather than a personal sentence. That hedge belongs to the source and is kept rather than upgraded.
stops.campa: At the end of 1511 he attends the schismatic council convened at Pisa by dissident cardinals with French and imperial backing against Julius II. By his own later account he was excommunicated for it, as, he says, a great many other theologians were. The German article carries that hedge, nach eigenem Bekunden, and cites no document behind it. The council collapses inside a few months and most of its participants are quietly forgiven. No page consulted records the sentence being lifted from him.
suggested_refs: The Conciliabulum of Pisa, 1511-1512, and its excommunications under Julius II

stops.name: Pavia, Plato and the Pimander
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology gives both courses with distinct subjects, the Symposium in 1512 and the Hermetic Pimander in 1515, and the German article agrees on Plato lectures from early 1512. The English article's bare '1515, Pimander' is a partial record, not a contradiction, and is not flagged as one. The doctorates in both laws and in medicine are reported status; no surviving university record proves either.
stops.campa: He lectures publicly at the University of Pavia: in 1512 on Plato's Symposium, in 1515 on the Pimander, the first treatise of the Hermetic writings that Ficino had put into Latin fifty years before. One course is on love, the other on the ascent of the soul, and both are handled as technical subjects with rules. He is credited in the sources with doctorates in both laws and in medicine, and no university record proves either. Students turn up, the fees are paid, and he holds the lectern until 1515.
stops.quote: Magick is a faculty of wonderfull vertue, full of most high mysteries, containing the most profound Contemplation of most secret things, together with the nature, power, quality, substance, and vertues thereof, as also the knowledge of whole nature...
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, Book 1, Chapter 2, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Ficino's Latin Pimander (1471) and the Hermetic corpus as university lecture material

stops.name: Pavia, the marriage and the army on the Ticino
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the marriage: a Pavia wife c.1515 rests on specialist reconstruction and is consistent with the independently attested Italian chronology, but her name appears in no page consulted. Attested: that the French victory at Marignano forced him out of teaching at Pavia (Stanford Encyclopedia), and that he fled toward Piedmont with his wife at the end of 1515 (German Wikipedia). The flight is narrated at the Pavia pin rather than at an invented waypoint.
stops.campa: He marries a woman of Pavia. Her name does not survive in any page consulted, only that she was Italian, that the marriage was by every account a happy one, and that she will be on the road with him before the year is out. He is twenty-eight, lecturing to paying students, drawing on doctorates he is said to hold, and for the only sustained stretch of his adult life he is not running from anything. In September the French win at Marignano. In December the army comes down the Ticino, the university empties, and the household loads what it can carry and turns west for Piedmont.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The Battle of Marignano, 13-14 September 1515, and the French reoccupation of Lombardy

stops.name: Casale Monferrato, the dedications to the Marquis
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology for the two dedications and their addressee, William IX Palaeologus, Marquis of Montferrat. The works list is standard bibliography and was not independently re-fetched. Whether the dedications produced any patronage is not recorded anywhere consulted. No month is given.
stops.campa: At Casale, seat of the Marquisate of Montferrat, he does what a scholar without a salary does. He writes two short treatises and puts a nobleman's name on the front of each. The Dialogus de homine and the De triplici ratione cognoscendi Deum go to William IX Palaeologus, Marquis of Montferrat, with the compliments and the implied invoice. The second argues that God is known three ways, by the book of nature, by the law, and by the gospel. Montferrat reads them, or does not. No appointment follows.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Agrippa, Dialogus de homine and De triplici ratione cognoscendi Deum (1516)

stops.name: Turin, lecturing without a post
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology that he lectured at Turin c.1516-1518 on theological subjects and failed to obtain a durable court appointment from the House of Savoy. No month or precise year within the bracket is recorded; 1517 orders the segment.
stops.campa: He moves on to Turin and lectures on theology, still hunting the durable Savoyard appointment that does not come. The Stanford chronology brackets the Turin years loosely, c.1516 to 1518, and records no post at the end of them. Seven years in Italy end the way they began: a man of thirty-one with a folded draft of an unpublishable book, several dedications outstanding, an Italian wife, and no salary. The offer, when it comes, comes from Metz, four hundred miles north.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The University of Turin and Savoyard court patronage in the 1510s

stops.name: Metz, orator of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested: the German Wikipedia article gives February 1518 for the appointment as civic orator and legal adviser; the English article and the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology both confirm the Metz office.
stops.campa: In February the city of Metz takes him on as its orator and advocate: a salaried civic office, speaking for the town, advising it in law, standing up in its disputes. It is the best job he ever holds. Metz is a free imperial city with a large Dominican establishment and a council that likes its lawyers clever. Inside eighteen months he will have used the office to attack an inquisitor's procedure in open court and to intervene in a Paris theological quarrel about the marriages of Saint Anne. He resigns in January 1520.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The office of syndic and advocatus in the free imperial city of Metz

stops.name: Metz, the woman of Woippy
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology confirms the defence of a woman accused of witchcraft at Woippy, and the German Wikipedia article confirms Woippy, the Metz venue, and the inherited-guilt argument. The inquisitor's name is contradictory across the literature, Nicolas Savin against Claudius Salini or Claude Salin, and is deliberately not settled here; the Stanford entry and the French article name nobody. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: A peasant woman from the village of Woippy is brought before the Dominican inquisitor on a charge of witchcraft. Part of the case against her is that her mother was burned: the guilt is treated as inherited, the daughter convicted in advance by her blood. Agrippa appears as her defender and goes straight at that reasoning, as a lawyer, on the procedure rather than on the theology. She is not executed. The inquisitor's name is given as Nicolas Savin in one line of the literature and as Claude Salin in another, and no source consulted settles which man it was.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The Woippy witchcraft case of 1519 and Agrippa's procedural defence

stops.name: Metz, the monogamy of Saint Anne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Metz Saint Anne controversy and Agrippa's support for Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples are reported in specialist synthesis and are consistent with the attested Metz timeframe, but were not independently confirmed in any page consulted. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples has argued that Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin, married once and not three times, against a devotional tradition that gave her three husbands and three daughters. Agrippa writes in his support: De beatissimae Annae monogamia, scripture set against custom. The mendicant preachers of Metz, who hold the cult of Saint Anne and the congregations that keep it, answer from the pulpits with the word heresy. Franciscans had used the same word against him at Ghent nine years earlier, for the opposite reason. The tract itself waits fifteen years to be printed.
suggested_refs: Agrippa, De beatissimae Annae monogamia (1519, printed 1534)
The Lefevre d'Etaples controversy over the trinubium of Saint Anne

stops.name: Metz, the twenty-fifth of January
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure from Metz on 25 January 1520, and arrival at Cologne by July 1520, per the German Wikipedia article. The English article gives only the year of resignation. The more specific record is followed.
stops.campa: He leaves Metz on the twenty-fifth of January, the office resigned under pressure from the friars, two years into the only steady employment of his life. He is thirty-three, with a wife, a small child, and a manuscript no printer will touch. The English article records only that he resigned in 1520. The German article gives the day of departure and puts him at Cologne by July, and after Cologne the next fifteen years run Geneva, Fribourg, Lyon, Antwerp, Mechelen, Brussels, Bonn.
suggested_refs: The Metz municipal records of Agrippa's tenure and resignation

stops.name: Cologne, Hutten and the abbot's papers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Cologne stay and the meeting with Ulrich von Hutten, July 1520 (German Wikipedia). The transfer of Trithemius's magical manuscripts in 1520 is dated by the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology and is carried in johannes_trithemius.journey.json, whose own stop marks the PLACE as an explicit reconstruction pinned to Cologne as a guess. The year is attested; the city is not.
stops.campa: Back in the city he was born in, he meets Ulrich von Hutten, the imperial knight who is at that moment writing Latin invective against Rome faster than the presses can take it. Trithemius's magical manuscripts, the abbot dead at Wurzburg four years earlier, pass into his hands. Where the handover happened is not recorded and Cologne is a guess. He will work the papers into the revision of his own book across the next twelve years, adding, correcting, hedging.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
johannes_trithemius.journey.json, stop 'Cologne, the manuscripts change hands'
suggested_refs: Trithemius's Steganographia and the manuscript corpus that reached Agrippa in 1520

stops.name: Geneva, the licence to practise
stops.date_confidence: attested that he practised medicine at Geneva from 1521, with a licence and hospital-connected work (English Wikipedia; Stanford Encyclopedia chronology). The absence of a documented medical degree follows the same sources' treatment of the Pavia doctorates. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: He arrives at Geneva and becomes a physician. There is no medical degree in the record, only the doctorate he is said to hold, a licence the city grants him, and work attached to the hospital. Medicine in 1521 is Galen, astrology, and the pharmacy of the countryside, and a man who has written three books on the sympathies binding herbs, stars, and organs is not obviously unqualified for it. Nobody in Geneva appears to have asked to see a diploma. He treats the sick of the city for two years.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: The Hotel-Dieu of Geneva and municipal medical licensing in the 1520s

stops.name: Geneva, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested: the German Wikipedia article names Jana Luisa Tissie, gives her age as eighteen, and dates the marriage to the end of 1521. A synthesis placing it in the spring of 1521 is supported by no source consulted and is not followed; the conflict is recorded rather than carried. The name is spelled variously in the correspondence, including Iana Loysa Tytia.
stops.campa: At the end of the year he marries again. She is Jana Luisa Tissie, eighteen years old, of Geneva; he is thirty-five and a widower with a child. The correspondence records her name in three or four spellings, and records him, over the next eight years, as unusually attached to her. She will follow him to Fribourg, to Lyon, and across a war frontier into the Low Countries, bear him children in each place, and die of plague at Antwerp before she is thirty.
suggested_refs: Agrippa's Epistolae, the source for the household's movements 1521-1529

stops.name: Fribourg, city physician for a season
stops.date_confidence: attested: city physician of Fribourg in 1523, resigned July 1523, per the German Wikipedia article, which contradicts the English article's loose 'until 1524'. Combined with the confirmed May 1524 arrival at Lyon, the tenure ran roughly four months with a gap afterwards; a synthesis giving 'March-July 1523, roughly six months' is arithmetically wrong. The reason for leaving is not documented and the possibilities named in the campa are candidates, not findings.
stops.campa: Fribourg appoints him city physician in the spring. He resigns in July. Four months, and then most of a year unaccounted for before he surfaces at Lyon: whether he was pushed, whether the Catholic canton's ban on Lutheran books touched a man who owned a library, or whether he had simply heard that the regent of France was hiring, nothing in the record says. The English article's loose 'until 1524' is contradicted by the July resignation the German article records.
suggested_refs: Fribourg's 1523 municipal ban on Lutheran books

stops.name: Lyon, physician to the regent
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology and the German Wikipedia article both give May 1524 and the appointment as physician to Louise of Savoy, mother of Francis I and regent of France during his Italian campaign.
stops.campa: In May he reaches Lyon, the wartime seat of the French government, as physician to Louise of Savoy: mother of Francis I, and regent of France while her son campaigns in Italy. It is the highest place he ever stands: a court appointment, a pension on the books, and daily access to the woman running the kingdom. Within a year Francis will be a prisoner in Madrid, the treasury will be raising a king's ransom, and the pension list will be cut. He draws his until 1526.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Louise of Savoy's regency household at Lyon, 1524-1526

stops.name: Lyon, the horoscope refused and the vanity written
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology confirms that De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium was composed in 1526 during a period of pension removal and travel restriction. NOT confirmed in any source consulted: the horoscope refusal itself, its stated canon-law reasoning, and the October 1526 date for the pension cancellation. All three come from specialist synthesis and are carried here as reconstruction. The English article gives composition and printing as 1526-1527, the Stanford chronology gives 1530 for publication.
stops.campa: The regent wants a judicial horoscope cast for her son: what will happen to Francis, and when. Agrippa refuses. Predicting the future of a named individual from the stars is superstition and contrary to canon law, he says, and he says it to the woman who pays him. He is struck off the pension list, forbidden to leave the city, and left in debt. That summer, in a town he is not allowed to quit, he writes De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium. It works through the sciences one chapter at a time, every one of them, his own included.
stops.quote: And therefore quite contrary to what has been hitherto practized, my Opinion is, That these Arts and Sciences are so far from being to be extoll'd with such high applauses and Panegyricks, that they are rather for the most part to be disprais'd and vilifi'd
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, Of the Vanity of Arts and Sciences, Chapter 1, English translation (London, 1676; text also checked against the 1694 edition)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, Of the Vanity of Arts and Sciences, archive.org items vanityartsandsc00unkngoog and b30332199
suggested_refs: Agrippa, De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium, composed Lyon 1526

segments.name: Antwerp, Mechelen, and the Book That Sold

stops.name: Antwerp, across the frontier
stops.date_confidence: attested: the English Wikipedia article gives 1528 for giving up the Louise of Savoy post, and the German article puts the arrival at Antwerp at the end of 1528. The July 1528 departure from Lyon and the war-disrupted crossing are given only by specialist synthesis and are not independently confirmed; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He gives up the French post and takes his family north to Antwerp, across a frontier disrupted by the war between Valois and Habsburg. Antwerp in 1528 is the richest port in Europe and the freest printing town north of Venice, and that is the point of going: he is carrying two finished manuscripts nobody in France would set in type, the three books of occult philosophy and the attack on the sciences. He practises medicine to feed the household while he hunts a printer and a patron, and finds, briefly, both.
suggested_refs: The Antwerp printing trade of the 1520s and its tolerance of condemned texts

stops.name: Antwerp, the plague
stops.date_confidence: attested: the German Wikipedia article gives death by plague on 17 August 1529, shortly after childbirth. A March 1529 date circulates in one synthesis and is supported by no source consulted; August is followed and the conflict is recorded rather than presented as unresolved.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of August his wife dies of plague, shortly after giving birth. Eight years of marriage; she is not yet thirty. He is left in a foreign city with the children, the epidemic still running in the streets outside, and the manuscripts still unprinted. The German article gives the day flatly; a March date circulates elsewhere with nothing behind it. He goes on treating plague patients through the rest of the outbreak, and the letters he writes that autumn survive in the collected Epistolae.
suggested_refs: The Antwerp plague of 1529
Agrippa's Epistolae, the letters of autumn 1529

stops.name: Mechelen, archivist and historiographer
stops.date_confidence: attested: the German Wikipedia article has him taking up the post of imperial archivist and historiographer at Mechelen in 1529. The English article places the office vaguely in the 1530s, and one reconstruction gives 27 December 1529, a day confirmed by no source consulted; 1529 is used unqualified and the day is dropped. Margaret of Austria's death at Mechelen on 1 December 1530 is independently attested. The Bologna coronation account is [R], from the standard works list.
stops.campa: Margaret of Austria, regent of the Habsburg Netherlands, the same Margaret whose court at Ghent heard him denounced twenty years before, takes him on at Mechelen as imperial archivist and historiographer to Charles V. A salary is granted, and whether any of it reached him the pages consulted do not show. He writes the official account of the emperor's coronation at Bologna. When Margaret dies at Mechelen on the first of December 1530, he writes her funeral oration.
sources: Wikipedia (en), 'Margaret of Austria, Duchess of Savoy'
suggested_refs: The Hof van Savoye at Mechelen, Margaret of Austria's court

stops.name: Antwerp, De vanitate in print
stops.date_confidence: attested: the English Wikipedia article gives the Antwerp printing of De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium in 1530, and the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology gives 1530 for the publication and its condemnation. Some accounts also record a 1531 issue. Composition was 1526; the English translation quoted here is the seventeenth-century one. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: The book written in disgrace at Lyon four years earlier is printed at Antwerp. Every art and science in turn: grammar, law, medicine, astrology, theology, the courtier's trade, magic itself, each taken up and found empty, the whole ending in an appeal to the plain word of scripture. It is savage and it is funny, and it sells better than anything else he writes. Some accounts record a second issue the following year. Translations follow through the century into French, English, and Italian.
stops.quote: Nothing can happen more Pestilential to Man, than Knowledge: this is that true Plague that invades all Mankind with so much confusion
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, Of the Vanity of Arts and Sciences, Chapter 1, English translation (London, 1676; text also checked against the 1694 edition)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, Of the Vanity of Arts and Sciences, archive.org items vanityartsandsc00unkngoog and b30332199
suggested_refs: The 1530 Antwerp editio princeps of De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium

stops.name: Brussels, imprisoned for debt
stops.date_confidence: attested: both the English and German Wikipedia articles name Brussels for the debt imprisonment at the end of 1530, in preference to the vaguer 'in the Netherlands' of synthesis. The additional detail that his books were publicly burned around the same time is single-sourced to the German article and could not be corroborated. No day is recorded.
stops.campa: He is jailed at Brussels for debt. It is a short imprisonment and it is not the last threat of one; creditors will still be the reason he runs, two years from now. The German article adds that his books are publicly burned at about the same time, a detail no other page consulted repeats. In the same winter he holds an imperial court title and has a printed bestseller on the stalls of two countries. The title carries no reliable money and the printer keeps the profits.
suggested_refs: Debt imprisonment in the Habsburg Netherlands and the finances of court appointment

stops.name: Mechelen, condemned at Louvain and at Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia entry states that De vanitate was condemned by Louvain AND by the Sorbonne; the Paris condemnation is missing from the syntheses that name only Louvain and is restored here. The Great Council of Mechelen proceedings and the formal dismissal from court employment are NOT independently confirmed and are carried as reconstruction. Sources consulted disagree on how firmly this episode is established. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: The Faculty of Theology at Louvain condemns De vanitate as scandalous, impious, and heretical. The Sorbonne condemns it too. Both bodies are reading a book that attacks theology as a science, so the verdict surprises nobody, least of all the author, who has the defence written before the censure lands. The Great Council of Mechelen is said to have taken the matter up and to have put him out of the emperor's service over it, ending four years of Habsburg employment. That half of the story rests on synthesis and on no page consulted here.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Agrippa, Apologia adversus calumnias ... propter declamationem de vanitate scientiarum (1533)

segments.name: Bonn, and the Book Printed at Last

stops.name: Bonn, the archbishop's household
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hermann von Wied, archbishop-elector of Cologne, received him into his household in 1532 (Stanford Encyclopedia; German Wikipedia; corroborated at the English article on Johann Weyer). MONTH CONTRADICTED between two independent sources: the Stanford chronology gives June 1532, the German article gives 'Ab Marz 1532', some months at the archbishop's country estate. Neither is preferred; March is used only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Hermann von Wied, archbishop and elector of Cologne, takes him into his household at Bonn. It is refuge from creditors and from the courts of the Netherlands, and it is also the first patron in his life who wants the occult philosophy printed rather than suppressed. Hermann is a reforming prince who will one day be excommunicated himself for trying to bring Lutheran preaching into the Rhineland; sheltering a condemned magician sits well within his range. Agrippa dedicates the complete De occulta philosophia to him.
stops.quote: Such is the greatness of your renowned fame (most reverend, and Illustrious Prince)...
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, dedicatory epistle to Hermann von Wied, Archbishop and Elector of Cologne, prefixed to De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, dedicatory epistle, trans. John French (1651)
suggested_refs: Hermann von Wied's reform of the archdiocese of Cologne and his 1546 excommunication

stops.name: Cologne, Soter sets the type
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology dates Johannes Soter's typesetting of the complete work to November 1532 and names the printer. The separate 1531 printing of Book I is given by the English Wikipedia article on De occulta philosophia libri tres as Paris, Cologne, and Antwerp, three cities; the Stanford entry names only Cologne. The commonly circulated 'Antwerp and Paris' omits Cologne.
stops.campa: In November the printer Johannes Soter begins setting the complete De occulta philosophia libri tres at Cologne. Book one had already gone out on its own the year before, printed at Paris, at Antwerp, and here. This is the whole system: twenty-two years after the draft went to Wurzburg, revised, expanded, and fenced about with cautions the young man had not thought necessary. The first sentence of book one is still the sentence he wrote at twenty-three.
stops.quote: Seeing there is a three fold World, Elementary, Celestiall, and Intellectuall, and every inferior is governed by its superior, and receiveth the influence of the vertues thereof...
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, Book 1, Chapter 1, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (1651), esotericarchives.com
suggested_refs: Johannes Soter's Cologne press
The 1531 separate printing of Book I at Paris, Cologne, and Antwerp

stops.name: Cologne, the inquisitor and the Senate
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology names the Dominican Conrad Kollin, dates the denunciation to December 1532, and records Hermann von Wied's intervention and the compulsory appendix. A protest letter dated 11 January 1533 appears in synthesis and is confirmed by no source consulted; the December dating is followed and the January date dropped. The quote is from Agrippa's own 1510 letter to Trithemius on why magic has fallen into disrepute, printed at the front of the very volume under suspension.
stops.campa: In December the Dominican Conrad Kollin, inquisitor at Cologne, reads the sheets and denounces the book as heretical and blasphemous. The city Senate suspends the printing. Agrippa protests in writing that the proceeding is illegal, the archbishop-elector intervenes over the Senate's head, and the press restarts on one condition: the volume must carry an appendix drawn from the anti-magic chapters of De vanitate, in which the author disowns what the three books in front of it have just built.
stops.quote: Now the cause, as I conceive is no other then this, viz. because by a certain fatall depravation of times, and men, many false Philosophers crept in, and these under the name of Magicians, heaping together through various sorts of errors and factions of false Religions, many cursed superstitions and dangerous Rites, and many wicked Sacrileges, out of Orthodox Religion...
stops.quote_source: Agrippa to Johannes Trithemius (1510), prefatory correspondence to De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, prefatory correspondence, trans. John French (1651)
suggested_refs: Conrad Kollin, Dominican inquisitor of Cologne
The De vanitate appendix bound into the 1533 edition

stops.name: Cologne, the three books complete
stops.date_confidence: attested: the complete De occulta philosophia libri tres was published at Cologne in 1533, printer Johannes Soter, after Hermann von Wied overrode the Senate's ban (English Wikipedia; Stanford Encyclopedia chronology, which also notes that his surviving correspondence ends in July 1533). The month is taken from that endpoint and orders the segment.
stops.campa: The complete De occulta philosophia libri tres appears at Cologne. Three books: the elemental world of stones, herbs, and animals; the celestial world of number, proportion, and the images of the stars; the intellectual world of the divine names, the orders of angels, and the ascent of the soul. It is the fullest statement of Renaissance magic in print, and it goes out with a chapter bound in at the back saying that magic is worthless. Both halves are his. He never explains.
stops.quote: I do not doubt but the Title of our book of Occult Philosophy, or of Magick, may by the rarity of it allure many to read it...
stops.quote_source: Agrippa, preface 'To the Reader', De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (London, 1651)
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
Agrippa, De Occulta Philosophia, trans. John French (1651), esotericarchives.com
suggested_refs: Vittoria Perrone Compagni's critical Latin edition, Brill, 1992
The 1651 English translation attributed to 'J.F.', printed by R.W. for Gregory Moule, London
Eric Purdue's complete translation, Inner Traditions, 2021, and Paul Summers Young's, Black Letter Press, 2020
Willis F. Whitehead's 1898 Chicago edition, packaging Henry Morley's 1856 biography with magic-mirror instructions
Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964), and the Nauert-Zambelli-Perrone Compagni rehabilitation

stops.name: Bonn, the memorandum to the Parliament
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to particulars: the Stanford Encyclopedia chronology confirms a 1534 legal memorandum sent from Bonn to the Parliament of the Low Countries. Synthesis describes the addressee instead as 'the Mechelen tribunal' and dates the document 22 February 1534; neither the addressee nor the day is confirmed by any source consulted. The date is retained only to order the segment.
stops.campa: From Bonn he sends a legal memorandum to the Parliament of the Low Countries, arguing once more that the proceedings taken against him were illegal and the procedure unfair. He is forty-seven, sheltered by an archbishop, with the book of his life at last in print and a condemnation bound into the front of it. The argument he files is on procedure and not on doctrine, which is where he had put it for the woman of Woippy fifteen years before. It is the last document of his that anyone has dated.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Agrippa's printed Epistolae, whose last dated items belong to the Bonn years

stops.name: Lyon, arrested on the king's order
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stanford Encyclopedia entry states that he was arrested by order of Francis I upon his return to France, and that he was released. NOT confirmed by any source consulted: that the arrest happened at Lyon, that the cause was insults to Louise of Savoy printed in De vanitate, that Johann Weyer is the testifying source, or that friends secured the release. The Lyon pin is itself a reconstruction, used because no other city is named. Year given variously as 1534 or 1535.
stops.campa: He crosses back into France and is arrested on the order of Francis I. Where, on what charge, and how he got out again are all reported and none of it confirmed: that it happened at Lyon, that the cause was the insults to Louise of Savoy printed in De vanitate, that Johann Weyer, his own pupil and housemate, is the source for the story, that friends bought or argued him free. The Stanford entry holds only that he was arrested on the king's order and that he was released. Even the year moves, 1534 in some accounts and 1535 in others.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Johann Weyer's near-contemporary testimony about his teacher's last year

stops.name: Grenoble, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: Grenoble is confirmed by all four sources consulted. Three of the four, the English, German, and French Wikipedia articles, give 18 February 1535, aged 48; the Stanford Encyclopedia entry alone hedges to 1535 'or, at the latest, in 1536'. The specific day is followed and the hedge recorded. Coordinates are held consistent with the burial and legend stops at 45.1885, 5.7245.
stops.campa: He dies at Grenoble in the Dauphine, forty-eight years old, weeks or months after the arrest. The English, German, and French accounts give the eighteenth of February 1535; the Stanford entry will say only 1535, or at the latest 1536. He has held one salaried office for two full years and every other for less. He has been called a heretic by two orders and has buried two wives. Both of his books are in print, the magic and the attack on learning, and they contradict each other. Three sons survive him.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
suggested_refs: Grenoble in the Dauphine, 1535, and the absence of any death record for Agrippa

stops.name: Grenoble, the black dog
stops.date_confidence: legend, not biography: reconstruction throughout. Paolo Giovio's Elogia and Johannes Manlius's 1563 commonplace book as the print origins were not independently verified. Gabriel Naude's 1625 Apologie is confirmed via the French Wikipedia article, which also shows that Naude places the death at LYON, contradicting the Grenoble burial tradition; the contradiction is recorded, not resolved. Johann Weyer's reported denial was not found in the pages consulted. Dated to the deathbed only to place the scene.
stops.campa: Within a generation the deathbed acquires a scene. Paolo Giovio's hostile Elogia and a 1563 commonplace book out of Melanchthon's circle turn the black dog he kept as a pet into a familiar spirit. Gabriel Naude prints the finished version in 1625: the dying man poor and abandoned by everyone, tearing off a collar full of magical figures and driving the animal into a river. The name meanwhile passes into the Faust legend. Johann Weyer, who lived in the house, said it was a dog.
stops.quote: will be as cunning as Agrippa was, / Whose shadow made all Europe honour him
stops.quote_source: Christopher Marlowe, The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus, Act 1 Scene 1 (Project Gutenberg e-text 811)
sources: Wikipedia (fr), 'Cornelius Agrippa', quoting Naude's Apologie pour les grands hommes soupconnez de magie (1625)
Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus, Project Gutenberg e-text 811
suggested_refs: Paolo Giovio, Elogia virorum literis illustrium
Johannes Manlius, Locorum communium collectanea (1563)
Johann Weyer, De praestigiis daemonum, on his teacher's household

stops.name: Grenoble, buried among the Dominicans
stops.date_confidence: attested by the German Wikipedia article, which gives the Dominican-convent burial, the gravestone inscription naming Hades as the fitting place for Agrippa, and the stone's passage between several monasteries for safekeeping until its trail is lost. Syntheses that add Cerberus to the inscription are not supported by that source, and the addition is dropped. Neither the English article nor the Stanford entry mentions the burial at all. No burial date is recorded; 20 February orders the sequence.
stops.campa: He is buried in the church of the Dominican convent at Grenoble, the order that had denounced him at Metz and again at Cologne. The gravestone carries an inscription saying that the fitting place for Agrippa would be Hades. Afterwards the stone is carried from one monastery to another for safekeeping, and at some point the record of where it went simply stops. Which house held it last, no page consulted says. No grave survives to visit and no burial register names him.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent church of Grenoble and the lost Agrippa gravestone

stops.name: Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, the sons
stops.date_confidence: attested by the German Wikipedia article that three sons survived him and became citizens of Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye in the Isere; the surname form Corneille-Agrippa is corroborated by specialist synthesis working from French court records, where the place appears as Saint-Antoine-de-Viennois. Coordinates corrected to Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, Isere (45.1758, 5.2172), roughly 9 km from the point that circulates. No date is recorded; 1540 orders the sequence.
stops.campa: Three sons outlive him and become citizens of Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye in the Isere, some forty kilometres from where their father died. They do not carry the Nettesheim name forward. In the French records they appear as Corneille-Agrippa, the toponym dropped and the Latin praenomen turned into a surname, which is what happens to a foreign name in a French village inside one generation. Whatever library, papers, or debts he left behind, no inventory of any of it turns up in a page consulted.
suggested_refs: French court records naming the sons at Saint-Antoine-de-Viennois under the surname Corneille-Agrippa

stops.name: Grenoble, the church pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested by the German Wikipedia article that the Dominican church at Grenoble was destroyed by Protestants in 1562. No primary confirmation of that specific church's destruction was obtained, and no month is recorded.
stops.campa: In 1562 Huguenot forces sack the religious houses of Grenoble and the Dominican church is destroyed. It is the first year of the French Wars of Religion. The German article is the only page consulted that records the destruction. Whatever remained of the tomb goes with the building, twenty-seven years after the burial. The stone had already been carried out for safekeeping by then, so the lost trail of the stone and the lost site of the church are two separate losses rather than one. Nothing marks the place.
suggested_refs: The 1562 Huguenot sack of Grenoble's religious houses

stops.name: Cologne, a figure on the tower
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the statue is attested by a captioned photograph on the French Wikipedia article, which corroborates the Fygen Lutzenkirchen adjacency exactly, but neither the German article on the Kolner Rathaus nor the English one lists Agrippa among named figures, and neither enumerates the full roster. The German article dates the figure programme 1988-1995, records all figures removed in 2006 after a conservation failure, and replaced in Savonniere stone from July 2008. So 1988 is the programme's start year, not an installation date, and any figure standing there now is a post-2008 replacement. The Apollinaire and Shelley references are attested from the primary texts.
stops.campa: The city hall tower of Cologne is fitted with a hundred and twenty-four stone figures of citizens the city claims for itself. One of them is Agrippa, standing beside the silk merchant Fygen Lutzenkirchen. Four and a half centuries after Ghent, Louvain, Paris, and Cologne itself condemned him in turn, the town whose Latin name he carried puts him on its own front wall. Mary Shelley had already handed the boy Victor Frankenstein a volume of Cornelius Agrippa to find, and handed his father one line about it: sad trash.
stops.quote: O Corneille Agrippa l'odeur d'un petit chien m'eut suffi / Pour decrire exactement tes concitoyens de Cologne
sources: Wikipedia (fr), 'Cornelius Agrippa' (captioned photograph of the Rathausturm statue)
Mary Shelley, Frankenstein, chapters 2-3, Project Gutenberg e-text 84
suggested_refs: The Rathausturm figure programme, Cologne, and its unenumerated roster of 124
Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818), chapters 2-3, on Victor's reading of Agrippa and Paracelsus
